extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, damages experts, and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Appellate-level guidance and legal standards for evaluating patent infringement, claim construction, written-description validity, damages methodology (reasonable royalty/hypothetical negotiation), expert testimony admissibility, and standards of review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial judge gatekeeping under Daubert
rubrics_metrics.description: The trial judge plays a 'gatekeeping role' to 'ensure that any and all scientific testimony or evidence admitted is not only relevant, but reliable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodology must be reasonable and its data or evidence sufficiently tied to the facts of the case to satisfy the gatekeeping role. (Quoting Daubert; discussing EcoFactor v. Google and Apple v. Wi‑LAN.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review for district court damages methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: We review a district court’s decision concerning the methodology for calculating damages for an abuse of discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate courts defer to the district court's gatekeeping and methodological rulings unless there is an abuse of discretion (citing Apple Inc. v. Wi‑LAN).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothetical negotiation (reasonable royalty) approach
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothetical negotiation approach attempts to calculate the royalty rate the parties would have agreed upon had they negotiated an agreement prior to the start of the infringement (applies under 35 U.S.C. § 284).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties frequently rely on comparable license agreements when using the hypothetical negotiation approach; experts should tie comparables to the facts of the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparables must account for differences in technology and economics
rubrics_metrics.description: When relying on comparable licenses to prove a reasonable royalty, a party must 'account for differences in the technologies and economic circumstances of the contracting parties.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts must explain how comparables differ from the accused technology and parties (VirnetX citation). Failure to do so undermines reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment / allocation among licensed patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert testimony relying on a portfolio or lump‑sum license should allocate license fees among the licensed patents; testimony should be excluded when it fails to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portfolio licenses frequently cover many patents; experts must address the extent to which each patent (including the asserted patent(s)) contributed to the lump sum. Courts exclude opinions that fail to allocate (Jiaxing; Apple example where failure to address contribution of other patents rendered testimony unreliable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Must tie comparables to contribution of specific patents
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert relying on a comparable that licenses multiple 'asserted' patents must address the extent to which the other patents contributed to the royalty rate (cannot simply apply an arbitrary discount without factual tether).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Apple v. Wi‑LAN — expert's 25% reduction was untethered because he failed to analyze other 'Asserted Patents' in the comparable license; silence on equally situated patents makes opinion unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages must be proved, not guessed (no conjecture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages must not be left to conjecture by the jury; they must be proved and not guessed at. Section 284 does not require an award of damages if none are proven that adequately tie a dollar amount to the infringing acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There must be enough evidence to allow the factfinder to formulate a royalty; absence of evidence allowing apportionment or reasonable inference supports JMOL of no damages (citing Promega, TecSec, Devex).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff's burden and standards of proof for damages and invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff bears the burden to prove the amount of damages by a preponderance of the evidence; invalidity must be proved by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amount of damages is a factual finding (Promega); invalidity (e.g., for lack of written description) requires clear and convincing proof (Juno Therapeutics and general written‑description law).

rubrics_metrics.name: JMOL standard
rubrics_metrics.description: JMOL is proper when a party has been fully heard on an issue and there is no legally sufficient evidentiary basis for a reasonable jury to find for that party on that issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regional circuit law governs review of JMOL/new trial motions; Third Circuit reviews JMOL de novo and new trial for abuse of discretion. Courts must distinguish JMOL (granting no damages) from remittitur/conditional new trial (citing Promega, Steuben Foods, Lightning Lube).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial evidence standard for jury factual findings
rubrics_metrics.description: A factual finding is supported by substantial evidence if a reasonable jury could have found in favor of the prevailing party in light of the evidence presented at trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in reviewing jury determinations (e.g., infringement); appellate court will uphold if reasonable jury could have reached the conclusion on the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction: ordinary meaning and intrinsic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim terms are generally given their ordinary meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the art in question at the time of the invention; claim construction begins with the claim language and relies on intrinsic evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claim construction is decided solely on intrinsic evidence, review is de novo. Courts must avoid importing limitations from the specification into the claim (Phillips, Comput. Docking Station).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import limitations from embodiments/figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts will not countenance importing claim limitations from a few specification statements or figures into the claims, particularly if those extracts describe only embodiments of a broader claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single embodiment (e.g., an I‑beam shown in figures) does not limit a broader claim that does not recite that embodiment; avoid confining claims to disclosed embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning and effect of 'comprising'
rubrics_metrics.description: The transition 'comprising' creates a presumption that the recited elements are only part of the device and does not exclude additional, unrecited elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims using 'comprising' should be read to allow additional elements (e.g., an intervening shuttle) and not to require direct contact or exclude additional structure (Crystal Semiconductor, AFG Indus.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement is strict liability (no intent required)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct infringement does not require intent to infringe; it is a strict‑liability offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether the accused designer intended the accused function is immaterial to liability; focus is on whether accused product meets claim limitations (Trim‑Lok).

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement (35 U.S.C. § 112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must contain a written description that reasonably conveys to those skilled in the art that the inventor had possession of the claimed subject matter as of the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inquiry asks whether the disclosure reasonably conveys possession of the claimed invention; applicants are not required to describe every conceivable future embodiment. Written description is a question of fact (ScriptPro, Ariad, Rexnord, Moba).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparables must account for foreign and expired patents when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: When a comparable license covers foreign patents or expired patents (or patents not assertable in the forum), the expert should analyze whether those patents cover the same invention or products and how they contributed to the lump sum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to analyze foreign or expired patents (and their relationship to asserted U.S. patents) undermines apportionment and reliability; district courts may sensibly exclude or discount testimony that ignores such distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experts must tether general observations to case facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliance on general observations about other unrelated patent portfolios is unreliable unless tethered to the specific facts of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalized industry statements (e.g., 'most value is in the top patent') are insufficient; experts must perform fact‑specific allocation/analysis rather than rely on abstract portfolio heuristics (court criticized Kidder's 'most of the value' boilerplate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remittitur/new trial when reducing jury award
rubrics_metrics.description: When a court attempts to reduce a jury award because it believes the amount is not supported by the evidence, the plaintiff must be afforded the option of a new trial (conditional remittitur).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should distinguish between granting JMOL of no damages and remitting a jury award; conditional remittitur practice (Hetzel, Cortez) gives plaintiff the option to accept a lower award or take a new trial.
